The must-sees

  • Alcazaba

    Fortress

    It was built in the 11th century and enlarged under the Nasrids. Roman columns and capitals were reused in its gates.

    Look for: Notice how the gates turn sharply as you climb: bent entrances built to slow attackers down.

  • Atarazanas Market

    Market

    It was built in the 19th century on the site of a Nasrid shipyard, whose gate was kept. A large stained-glass window shows scenes of the city.

    Look for: On the Nasrid gate, look for shields carved with the dynasty’s motto: there is no victor but God.

  • Calle Larios

    Shopping · 1891

    It opened in 1891, funded by the Larios family and named after the Marquis. It links the port with Plaza de la Constitución.

    Look for: At the port end stands Mariano Benlliure’s bronze monument to the Marquis of Larios, on a tall stone pedestal.

  • Gibralfaro Castle

    Fortress

    Yusuf I of Granada built the castle in the 14th century to protect the Alcazaba. In 1487 it held out for months against the army of the Catholic Monarchs.

    Look for: Inside the walls, find the Airón well, cut deep into the rock to keep the garrison in water through a siege.

  • Málaga Cathedral

    Church

    Work began in 1528 and stopped in the 18th century before the south tower was completed. Locals call the building La Manquita, the one-armed lady.

    Look for: Inside, the carved cedar choir stalls include saints by the Baroque sculptor Pedro de Mena.

  • Picasso Museum Málaga

    Museum

    It opened in 2003 with works donated by the artist’s family. Phoenician and Roman remains are visible in the basement.

    Look for: Look up inside: several rooms keep the palace’s carved wooden coffered ceilings.

  • Roman Theatre

    Landmark

    It was built in the time of Augustus. It lay buried until 1951, when it was found during work on a cultural centre that was later demolished.

    Look for: Stand on Calle Alcazabilla: the Roman seats climb straight up toward the Moorish walls of the Alcazaba.

How it works

  1. Open Wizzy in Málaga and tap Start walk, or pick a ready-made walk.
  2. Put your phone in your pocket. Wizzy runs in the background, even with the screen locked.
  3. When you pass a place, you get a ping. Open it for the story, or keep walking.

Every place you see gets stamped in your Málaga passport. Your location stays on your phone. No ads, no tracking.
